items.title: Mapping a prior to the unit cube (for NS AW)
items.text:
The BlackJAX NS AW sampler requires the sampling space to be the unit hypercube [0, 1]^n_dims. The sample_transforms must map every parameter from its physical support into [0, 1]. get_default_sample_transforms(prior, ifos, space="unit_cube") builds all of the following for the standard prior types; the rest of this section shows what it does, for priors you handle yourself.

The key tool is BoundToBound, which linearly maps [a, b] → [c, d]:

from jimgw.core.transforms import BoundToBound

# Map chirp mass M_c ∈ [20, 80] to [0, 1]:
BoundToBound(
    name_mapping=(["M_c"], ["M_c_unit"]),
    original_lower_bound=20.0,
    original_upper_bound=80.0,
    target_lower_bound=0.0,
    target_upper_bound=1.0,
)

items.title: Parameters with bounded physical range
items.text:
Apply BoundToBound directly from the prior support to [0, 1]:

sample_transforms = [
    BoundToBound(name_mapping=(["M_c"], ["M_c_unit"]), original_lower_bound=M_c_min, original_upper_bound=M_c_max, target_lower_bound=0.0, target_upper_bound=1.0),
    BoundToBound(name_mapping=(["q"], ["q_unit"]),     original_lower_bound=q_min,   original_upper_bound=q_max,   target_lower_bound=0.0, target_upper_bound=1.0),
    # ... repeat for each bounded parameter
]

items.title: Angular parameters (sine / cosine priors)
items.text:
Angular parameters must be trigonometrically transformed first:

from jimgw.core.transforms import CosineTransform, SineTransform

sample_transforms += [
    CosineTransform(name_mapping=(["iota"], ["cos_iota"])),
    BoundToBound(name_mapping=(["cos_iota"], ["cos_iota_unit"]), original_lower_bound=-1.0, original_upper_bound=1.0, target_lower_bound=0.0, target_upper_bound=1.0),

    SineTransform(name_mapping=(["dec"], ["sin_dec"])),
    BoundToBound(name_mapping=(["sin_dec"], ["sin_dec_unit"]), original_lower_bound=-1.0, original_upper_bound=1.0, target_lower_bound=0.0, target_upper_bound=1.0),
]

items.title: Power-law priors (e.g. luminosity distance)
items.text:
For parameters with a power-law prior (not uniform), use the reversed PowerLawTransform so the sampling space is uniform on [0, 1]:

from jimgw.core.transforms import PowerLawTransform, reverse_bijective_transform

sample_transforms += [
    reverse_bijective_transform(
        PowerLawTransform(
            name_mapping=(["d_L_unit"], ["d_L"]),
            xmin=d_L_min,
            xmax=d_L_max,
            alpha=2.0,
        )
    ),
]

This maps d_L_unit ∈ [0, 1] (where the sampler works) back to d_L ∈ [d_L_min, d_L_max] with a d_L^2 prior, which is the volume-element prior for a uniformly distributed source population.

items.title: Rayleigh priors
items.text:
For parameters with a Rayleigh prior, use the reversed RayleighTransform:

from jimgw.core.transforms import RayleighTransform, reverse_bijective_transform

sample_transforms += [
    reverse_bijective_transform(
        RayleighTransform(
            name_mapping=(["x_unit"], ["x"]),
            sigma=0.5,
        )
    ),
]

items.title: Gaussian priors
items.text:
For parameters with a Gaussian prior, use the reversed GaussianTransform. The forward direction maps u ∈ (0, 1) to x = mu + sigma * ndtri(u) (probit function); the reverse direction is the normal CDF x → ndtr((x - mu) / sigma) ∈ (0, 1):

from jimgw.core.transforms import GaussianTransform, reverse_bijective_transform

sample_transforms += [
    reverse_bijective_transform(
        GaussianTransform(
            name_mapping=(["x_unit"], ["x"]),
            mu=0.0,
            sigma=1.0,
        )
    ),
]

items.title: Default transforms
items.text:
For standard compact-binary analyses you do not need to write the two lists yourself. jimgw.core.single_event.helpers derives them from your prior, the same way the CLI does:

from jimgw.core.single_event.helpers import (
    get_default_likelihood_transforms,
    get_default_sample_transforms,
)

# ifos must already have their data attached.
sample_transforms = get_default_sample_transforms(prior, ifos)
likelihood_transforms = get_default_likelihood_transforms(prior, ifos, waveform)

jim = Jim(
    likelihood,
    prior,
    sampler_config=FlowMCConfig(),
    sample_transforms=sample_transforms,
    likelihood_transforms=likelihood_transforms,
)
  • Sample transforms. t_c is sampled as the arrival time at ifos[0] and ra/dec as azimuth/zenith relative to the first two detectors. Pass detector_frame_time=False or detector_frame_sky=False to sample t_c or ra/dec directly.
  • Likelihood transforms. q to eta; J-frame spin angles and spherical spins to Cartesian spins; and a prior given in azimuth/zenith or t_det back to ra/dec and t_c.
  • NS AW. Pass space="unit_cube" to get_default_sample_transforms to map every sampled parameter to [0, 1] (see above for what that involves). This needs a prior made of UniformPrior, SinePrior, CosinePrior, PowerLawPrior, RayleighPrior and GaussianPrior. It also needs a t_det prior (or detector_frame_time=False) rather than t_c, because the delay between t_c and t_det depends on the sky position, so a t_c prior would not fill the unit interval exactly. Sampling ra/dec as azimuth/zenith additionally assumes an isotropic sky prior (ra uniform over one period, dec cosine); for any other sky prior, put the prior on azimuth/zenith directly or pass detector_frame_sky=False.
  • SMC. Pass space="unbounded" to map every sampled parameter that does not wrap around to the real line: its unit-cube map, then a logit, so each of these priors becomes a standard logistic distribution. Angles that wrap around (psi, phase_c, azimuth, ...) are left as they are; the SMC sampler handles them itself. A t_c prior sampled in the detector frame gives t_det the t_c range widened by 0.022 s on each side, the largest delay between the geocentre and a detector; the prior is zero outside the true range, so the result is still exact, though t_det is not exactly logistic near its edges.

These cover the common cases. For anything else, write the lists yourself as described above, or start from the default list and add to it.

items.title: Passing Transforms to Jim
items.text:
Both lists are passed to the Jim constructor:

from jimgw.core.jim import Jim
from jimgw.samplers.config import FlowMCConfig

jim = Jim(
    likelihood=likelihood,
    prior=prior,
    sampler_config=FlowMCConfig(),
    sample_transforms=sample_transforms,
    likelihood_transforms=likelihood_transforms,
)

Either list can be empty. If sample_transforms=[], the sampler operates directly in the prior space. If likelihood_transforms=[], the waveform is called with the prior parameters unchanged.

items.title: How-to
items.text:
Short recipes that each answer one "how do I ...?" question: the goal and the steps, nothing else.

  • Reduce GPU Memory Use — Which setting to lower, for each sampler, when the GPU runs out of memory.
  • Use Your Own Likelihood — Run Jim's samplers on a likelihood you write yourself, with or without Jim.

items.title: Use Your Own Likelihood
items.text:
Jim's samplers only need a function that returns a log-likelihood, so nothing here is specific to gravitational waves. There are two ways to use them with your own likelihood:

  • With Jim — when you want named parameters, priors and named results.
  • Without Jim — when you already have a log-density of a flat array and only want a sampler.

items.title: With Jim
items.text:
Subclass LikelihoodBase and implement evaluate. It receives a dictionary of parameter values and returns the log-likelihood:

import jax.numpy as jnp
from jimgw.core.base import LikelihoodBase


class SinusoidLikelihood(LikelihoodBase):
    def __init__(self, t, y, noise_std):
        self.t = jnp.asarray(t)
        self.y = jnp.asarray(y)
        self.noise_std = noise_std

    def evaluate(self, params):
        model = params["amplitude"] * jnp.sin(
            2 * jnp.pi * params["frequency"] * self.t + params["phase"]
        )
        return -0.5 * jnp.sum((self.y - model) ** 2) / self.noise_std**2

Give each parameter a prior with the same name, and pass both to Jim:

from jimgw.core.jim import Jim
from jimgw.core.prior import CombinePrior, UniformPrior
from jimgw.samplers.config import FlowMCConfig

prior = CombinePrior(
    [
        UniformPrior(0.0, 3.0, parameter_names=["amplitude"]),
        UniformPrior(3.0, 5.0, parameter_names=["frequency"]),
        UniformPrior(0.0, 6.28, parameter_names=["phase"]),
    ]
)

jim = Jim(
    SinusoidLikelihood(t, y, noise_std=0.5),
    prior,
    sampler_config=FlowMCConfig(n_chains=500, n_training_loops=10),
)
jim.sample()
samples = jim.get_samples()  # one array per parameter, plus "log_likelihood"

A complete script, with synthetic data and a corner plot, is examples/custom_likelihood.py.

Things to know

  • evaluate is compiled by JAX. Use jnp functions, and jnp.where or jax.lax.cond instead of a Python if on a parameter value, which raises TracerBoolConversionError.
  • Parameter names are not checked. The keys you read in evaluate must match the prior's parameter_names. A misspelt key raises KeyError when Jim is built, but a prior parameter that evaluate never reads is accepted without warning, and its posterior is just its prior.
  • Samplers and priors have their own constraints, such as a normalised prior or, for NS AW, the unit cube. They are listed in the sampler overview; the Transforms guide shows how to map a prior to the unit cube.
  • Importing Jim turns on 64-bit floats for all JAX code in the process, as a side effect of importing ripple. It matters if you rely on single precision.
  • Not available: the SwiG sampler, which needs a gravitational-wave likelihood with waveform caching, and the jim-run command, which cannot load a custom likelihood.

items.title: Without Jim
items.text:
build_sampler takes three functions of a flat array of shape (n_dims,): the log-prior, the log-likelihood and their sum. It does not import any gravitational-wave code and does not change the JAX float precision.

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jimgw.samplers import build_sampler
from jimgw.samplers.config import FlowMCConfig

lower = jnp.array([0.0, 3.0, 0.0])
upper = jnp.array([3.0, 5.0, 6.28])


def log_prior(x):
    inside = jnp.all((x > lower) & (x < upper))
    return jnp.where(inside, -jnp.sum(jnp.log(upper - lower)), -jnp.inf)


def log_likelihood(x):
    amplitude, frequency, phase = x
    model = amplitude * jnp.sin(2 * jnp.pi * frequency * t + phase)
    return -0.5 * jnp.sum((y - model) ** 2) / 0.5**2


config = FlowMCConfig(n_chains=500, n_training_loops=10)
sampler = build_sampler(
    config,
    n_dims=3,
    log_prior_fn=log_prior,
    log_likelihood_fn=log_likelihood,
    log_posterior_fn=lambda x: log_prior(x) + log_likelihood(x),
)

initial_position = lower + (upper - lower) * jax.random.uniform(
    jax.random.key(1), (config.n_chains, 3)
)
sampler.sample(jax.random.key(0), initial_position)
result = sampler.get_samples()  # "samples" of shape (n, 3) and "log_likelihood"

You provide the bounds, by returning -jnp.inf from log_prior outside them, and the starting points. The Samplers guide gives each sampler's config and how many starting points it needs.

items.title: Reduce GPU Memory Use
items.text: If a run fails because the GPU is out of memory, shrink how much work runs simultaneously. The right setting depends on which sampler backend you use.

items.title: flowMC (FlowMCConfig)
items.text:
flowMC has two independent memory bottlenecks:

  1. The NF proposal step — usually the bottleneck. During each global step, normalizing-flow proposals are generated for all chains at once. Reduce n_NFproposal_batch_size (default 1000); flowMC then evaluates the proposals in smaller jax.lax.map chunks instead of one big batch. Try this first.

  2. The local step — when the likelihood is very expensive. Sometimes the problem is not the NF proposals, but that even a single likelihood evaluation per chain across all n_chains chains will not fit. In that case also set chain_batch_size so chains are processed in sequential sub-batches of that size; smaller values use less memory. Sub-batching only happens when chain_batch_size is greater than 1 and less than n_chains; otherwise (including the default 0) all chains are processed in one vmap.

from jimgw.samplers.config import FlowMCConfig

jim = Jim(
    likelihood,
    prior,
    sampler_config=FlowMCConfig(
        n_chains=1000,
        n_NFproposal_batch_size=100,  # smaller NF-proposal batches (try this first)
        chain_batch_size=100,         # also batch chains if the likelihood alone is too big
        # ... other parameters
    ),
    ...
)

items.title: Technical Notes
items.text:
These notes give the details behind Jim's results: conventions and implementation choices that matter when you compare Jim with another code, but that the guides and how-tos do not need.

  • Detector Response Conventions — The phase convention of the finite-arm-length response and how to convert from the other common one.
  • Detector Presets — How the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer geometries are built.
  • Likelihood Details — Conventions of the data and the inner product, frequency ranges, time marginalisation, and how the fast likelihoods choose their bins and bands.
  • Signal-Duration Check — How inject_signal decides whether a signal fits the segment.
  • Sampler Details — How the SwiG sampler reuses the waveform, and how the SMC sampler moves its particles.

items.title: Detector Presets
items.text: get_H1(), get_L1() and get_V1() return single detectors with the site coordinates, arm azimuths and tilts written in jimgw/core/single_event/detector.py. get_ET(), get_ET_2L() and get_CE() return GroundBased3G detectors, which respond like GroundBased2G unless earth_rotation or finite_arm_length is switched on (see the data guide).

items.title: Einstein Telescope (Triangular detectors)
items.text: get_ET() returns three detectors, ET1, ET2 and ET3, with 10 km arms and 60 degrees between the two arms of each. ET1 is at the Euregio Meuse-Rhine site (about 50.723 N, 5.921 E, at zero elevation), the point of ET_EMR below, with its x-arm at the azimuth of the Virgo x-arm. ET2 and ET3 are the other two corners of an equilateral triangle with 10 km sides. Each corner is found by moving 10 km from the previous one in the direction of its x-arm, along a great circle (haversine formula) on a sphere whose radius is the WGS-84 radius at that latitude. The arms are rotated by 240 degrees from one corner to the next.

items.title: Einstein Telescope (2 L-shaped detectors)
items.text: get_ET_2L() returns two L-shaped detectors with 15 km arms and 90 degrees between the two arms of each: ET_Sar in Sardinia (about 40.517 N, 9.417 E) and ET_EMR in the Euregio Meuse-Rhine (about 50.723 N, 5.921 E), both at zero elevation. The sites and the way the angle is measured follow Branchesi et al. (2023). The arms of ET_Sar have the azimuths of the Virgo arms. Those of ET_EMR are rotated from them by alignment_angle, in degrees: 0 for parallel arms and 45 for the misaligned case of that paper. The default is 42.5. The rotation is a difference of azimuths, each measured against the local axes of its site rather than against the great circle between the sites. load_and_set_psd() sets the 15 km ET baseline ASD for them; see Default design-sensitivity ASD.

items.title: Cosmic Explorer
items.text: get_CE() returns one detector with 40 km arms at the LIGO Hanford site, with the coordinates, elevation and arm tilts of H1.

items.title: Sidereal angle
items.text:
The sky position is rotated into the Earth-fixed frame with the Greenwich mean sidereal time (GMST) at the trigger time of the data. This one angle sets both the antenna pattern and the delay between the geocentre and the detector. The coalescence time offset t_c only shifts the arrival time, so the angle is not advanced by t_c: for a signal with a non-zero t_c it is off by \(\omega_\oplus t_c\), where \(\omega_\oplus = 7.29 \times 10^{-5}\) rad/s is the rotation rate of the Earth. Bilby evaluates the angle at the arrival time at the geocentre, the trigger time plus t_c. For \(|t_c| \lesssim 0.1\) s the difference is below \(10^{-5}\) rad.

GroundBased3G detectors with earth_rotation=True follow the rotation across the signal. Each frequency then uses the angle at the time it was emitted,

\[\mathrm{GMST}(f) = \mathrm{GMST}_{\text{trigger}} + \omega_\oplus\,\bigl(t_c - \tau(f)\bigr),\]

with \(\tau(f)\) the time to merger of that frequency (GroundBased3G.time_to_merger). Here t_c is included.

items.title: Finite-arm-length phase convention
items.text:
The finite-arm-length response multiplies each arm's antenna pattern by a transfer function (Baral et al. 2023, Eq. 7), normalised so that it tends to one at low frequency. Its overall phase depends on which instant of the light's round trip in the arm the detector output is assigned to, and different codes make different choices. Jim uses this one:

  • The gravitational wave is referenced at the detector vertex, as for GroundBased2G.
  • The output is assigned to the time the light reaches the end mirror, i.e. half-way through its round trip, not to the time it returns to the beam splitter.

With \(x = fL/c\) for arm length \(L\), \(y = \mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{n}\) the projection of the propagation direction \(\mathbf{k}\) onto the arm \(\mathbf{n}\), and Jim's Fourier convention, in which a time delay \(\tau\) multiplies the frequency-domain signal by \(e^{-2\pi i f \tau}\), the transfer function is

\[T(f) = \frac{1}{2}\left[e^{-i\pi x(1+y)}\,\mathrm{sinc}\,x(1-y) + e^{i\pi x(1-y)}\,\mathrm{sinc}\,x(1+y)\right],\]

with \(\mathrm{sinc}\,z = \sin(\pi z)/(\pi z)\). At low frequency \(T \approx 1 - i\pi x y\), so it adds no direction-independent time delay to the long-wavelength response: injections made with or without the finite-arm-length response share the same time reference.

Codes that assign the output to the light's return at the beam splitter, following the round-trip construction of Rakhmanov et al. (2008), use

\[T_{\text{return}}(f) = e^{-2\pi i f L/c}\, T(f),\]

which delays the signal by \(L/c\): about 33 μs for the 10 km arms of ET and 133 μs for the 40 km arms of CE. For one detector, or a network with equal arm lengths, the difference is absorbed into \(t_c\). For a network with unequal arm lengths, such as ET with CE, it changes the relative arrival times by about 100 μs and can shift the inferred sky position. Injecting and recovering with GroundBased3G is consistent; when the data come from another code, check which convention it uses and apply the factor above if they differ.

items.title: Fourier and noise-weighting conventions
items.text:
The frequency-domain data are the one-sided discrete Fourier transform of the windowed time series, multiplied by the time step \(\Delta t\). The window is not renormalised. The PSD \(S_n(f)\) is one-sided, in \(\mathrm{Hz}^{-1}\), and \(\Delta f = 1/T\) for a segment of duration \(T\). The noise-weighted inner product is

\[(a|b) = 4\,\Delta f \sum_k \mathrm{Re}\left[\frac{a^*(f_k)\,b(f_k)}{S_n(f_k)}\right],\]

summed over the frequency range of the likelihood. For each detector the log-likelihood is \((d|h) - \tfrac{1}{2}(h|h)\), without the term \(-\tfrac{1}{2}(d|d)\) that does not depend on the parameters, and the detectors are summed.

items.title: Frequency ranges
items.text:
The Nyquist frequency of the data is computed as \(1/(2\Delta t)\). For some sampling rates (744 Hz, for example) \(1/(1/f_s)\) is not exactly \(f_s\), so a range that ends at \(f_s/2\) is accepted if it equals the Nyquist frequency to a relative \(10^{-12}\), both for the data and for the likelihood. When f_max is not given, the likelihood ends at the upper end of the frequency range of the data, or at the highest frequency of the data if that is lower, so the last bin is not lost to that rounding.

Whitened data (Detector.whitened_frequency_domain_data and whitened_time_domain_data) use the frequency range of the data, not that of a likelihood; for data without a range, set data.frequency_bounds to limit them.

items.title: Time marginalisation
items.text:
With time_marginalization, the likelihood is averaged over a uniform prior on \(t_c\) in tc_range. The average is a sum over the samples of the FFT time grid that lie inside the range, each weighted by the time spacing \(1/(N\,\Delta f)\) of the FFT grid of length \(N\), divided by the width \(W\) of tc_range:

\[\ln \bar L = \ln \left[\frac{1}{W}\sum_{t_k \in \text{tc\_range}} \frac{L(t_k)}{N\,\Delta f}\right].\]

The evidence of a run with time marginalisation includes the prior on \(t_c\), normalised over tc_range, so it is comparable with a run that samples \(t_c\) with a uniform prior on the same range. The posterior of the other parameters does not depend on the normalisation.

items.title: Heterodyning (Relative binning)
items.text: HeterodynedTransientLikelihoodFD places the bin edges at equal steps of the phase of the reference waveform. That phase is modelled as the sum of five power laws in frequency, \((f/f_*)^{\gamma}\) with \(\gamma = -5/3, -2/3, 1, 5/3, 7/3\) (Zackay et al. 2018), which stand for the Newtonian chirp, the spin-orbit term, the coalescence time and the merger-ringdown. Each term is scaled so that it changes by at most \(2\pi\) rad over the frequency range, and the cumulative sum is divided into equal steps. With n_bins the number of steps is given; with epsilon (default 0.5 rad) it is the total phase divided by epsilon, rounded down, and at least 1. Bins where the reference waveform is zero, usually beyond the merger frequency, are removed.

items.title: Multi-banding
items.text:
MultibandedTransientLikelihoodFD follows Morisaki 2021. The bands have durations \(T, T/2, T/4, \ldots\), where \(T\) is the duration of the data. The first band starts at the lowest f_min of the detectors and the last band ends at the highest f_max, as in bilby.

The start of each next band is the lowest frequency for which, with the 22-mode time to merger \(\tau(f)\) of the reference chirp mass (rescaled by highest_mode) and \(L\) the accuracy_factor,

  • the signal still fits in the shorter duration: \(\tau + L\sqrt{-\mathrm{d}\tau/\mathrm{d}f} < T_{\text{band}} - t_{\text{offset}}\), and
  • the transition from the previous band is smooth: \(f - 1/\sqrt{-\mathrm{d}\tau/\mathrm{d}f} > f_{\text{previous}}\).

It is found by bisection. time_offset is the time from the earliest arrival time that the prior allows (allowing for the light travel time across the Earth) to the end of the segment, and delta_f_end is the frequency scale of the taper at the high-frequency end. Both are inferred from the prior on \(t_c\) when it is given: with \(t_{\text{end}}\) the time from the trigger to the end of the data and \(R_\oplus/c\) the light travel time across the Earth, time_offset is \(t_{\text{end}} - t_{c,\min} + R_\oplus/c\) and delta_f_end is \(100 / (t_{\text{end}} - t_{c,\max} - R_\oplus/c)\). Without such a prior they default to 2.12 s and 53 Hz, which assume that the data end 2 s after the trigger; for other segments they must be given.

items.title: SwiG waveform cache
items.text:
SwiG updates one block of parameters at a time. The likelihood gives the sampler a cache of the generated waveform polarizations. A block whose parameters change the waveform refreshes the cache, so the waveform is generated again. A block that only changes the projection onto the detectors reuses the cache.

When the waveform model supports analytic distance scaling, the luminosity distance is factored out of the waveform, so a d_L block reuses the cache. Otherwise a d_L block refreshes it like any other waveform parameter.

The likelihood decides which parameters the waveform depends on after the sample transforms, the likelihood transforms, the fixed parameters and the analytic marginalisation have been applied.

items.title: SMC mutation
items.text: At every temperature, the SMC sampler moves all particles together, in coordinates fitted to them. The steps below run once per temperature, inside the jitted SMC step.

items.title: Coordinates
items.text:
Each angle that wraps around is cut in the middle of the widest arc that holds no particle. The angle is rotated so that the cut sits at the ends of its period, then mapped to the real line with a logit. A mode that straddles the ends of the period therefore stays in one piece, and two modes half a period apart are kept apart by the cut. The cut is fixed during the temperature step, so the map is an exact change of coordinates.

With a flow, flowMC's masked-coupling rational-quadratic spline is then trained on the particles with NFModel.train_jit: the inputs are rescaled by their mean and standard deviation, and the flow trains for n_epochs with flowMC's optimizer (clipped AdamW). Every temperature step trains a newly initialised flow with a fresh optimizer. The kernel then moves the particles in the flow's latent space.

Every proposal is mapped back to the sampling space and evaluated with the posterior. The acceptance ratio includes the log-Jacobian of the map, so the particles target the tempered posterior exactly whatever the quality of the flow; a poor flow only lowers the acceptance rate.

items.title: t-pCN
items.text:
t-pCN (a preconditioned Crank-Nicolson move with a Student-t reference) first fits a Student-t distribution to the particles. For 24 degrees of freedom \( u\) between 1 and 1000, an expectation-maximization (EM) fit gives the centre \(\mu\) and scale matrix \(\Sigma = L L^ op\); the \( u\) with the highest likelihood is kept. A particle \(z\) then moves to

\[z' = \mu + \sqrt{1 - ho^2}\,(z - \mu) + ho \sqrt{W}\, L \epsilon,\]

with \(\epsilon\) standard normal and \(W\) inverse-gamma with shape \(( u + d)/2\) and scale \(( u + \delta)/2\), where \(\delta\) is the squared Mahalanobis distance of \(z\) from \(\mu\) and \(d\) the dimension. This move leaves the fitted Student-t distribution unchanged, so its density ratio replaces the proposal ratio: \( frac{1}{2}( u + d)\,[\log(1 + \delta'/ u) - \log(1 + \delta/ u)]\) is added to the log acceptance ratio. Where the particles follow the Student-t fit, large moves are accepted.

The step size \( ho\) starts at \(\min(2.38/\sqrt{d}, 0.99)\), which is also its cap. After step \(i\) it moves by \((i + 1)^{-3/4}\) times the difference between the mean acceptance probability and target_acceptance_rate, and it carries over to the next temperature step.

A temperature step ends once the particles' mean log posterior has not improved for \(n_ ext{patience}\,( ho_ ext{max}/ ho)^2\) steps, with \(n_ ext{patience}\) = n_patience_per_dim \( imes\, d\), or after n_max_per_dim \( imes\, d\) steps. The factor \(( ho_ ext{max}/ ho)^2\) waits longer while small steps make slow progress.

items.title: Gaussian random walk
items.text: The random walk proposes \(z + \sqrt{s}\, L \epsilon\), with \(L L^\top\) the covariance of the particles at the current temperature, for n_mcmc_steps_per_dim \(\times\, d\) steps. After each temperature step, \(s\) is multiplied by \(\exp[\text{gain}\,(\text{acceptance} - \text{target})]\).

items.title: Likelihood evaluations
items.text: Each temperature step evaluates the posterior of all \(N\) particles once at the start and once per MCMC step. BlackJAX evaluates the likelihood once more per step: persistent sampling re-evaluates the moved particles, and tempered SMC uses them to reweight. The adaptive tempered mode also evaluates the particles to choose the next temperature, and persistent sampling evaluates the initial particles. With \(S_t\) MCMC steps at temperature step \(t\), n_likelihood_evaluations is therefore \(N\,[1 + \sum_t (S_t + 2)]\) for the persistent modes, \(N \sum_t (S_t + 3)\) for the adaptive tempered mode, and \(N \sum_t (S_t + 2)\) for the fixed tempered mode.

items.title: Credits
items.text: The t-pCN move, its step-size adaptation and the plateau stopping rule follow minipcn (M. J. Williams), Grumitt et al. 2024 (arXiv:2407.07781) and pocoMC (Karamanis et al.).

items.title: Signal-Duration Check
items.text:
Detector.inject_signal checks, before it changes anything, that the signal fits the data segment around its peak. Parts of a signal that fall outside the segment would wrap around to the other end, because the injection is done in the frequency domain. If the signal does not fit, inject_signal raises a ValueError; with allow_wraparound=True it injects anyway and logs a warning.

The check does not evaluate the waveform. It estimates how long the signal lasts before and after its peak from the chirp mass, the symmetric mass ratio and the spins, and compares that with the position of the peak in the segment, trigger_time - start_time + t_c. The signal fits if

\[\text{peak} \ge T_{\text{before}} \quad\text{and}\quad \text{peak} + T_{\text{after}} \le \text{duration}.\]

items.title: The estimate
items.text:
With \(M\) the total mass in seconds (\(GM/c^3\)) and \(f_{\text{start}}\) the frequency at which the signal enters the frequency range of the data,

\[T_{\text{before}} = T_{\text{chirp}}(f_{\text{start}}) + 200\,M + \frac{1}{f_{\text{start}}} + \frac{R_\oplus}{c}, \qquad T_{\text{after}} = 1000\,M + \frac{1}{f_{\text{start}}} + \frac{R_\oplus}{c}.\]
  • Chirp time. The 2PN inspiral time from XLALSimInspiralChirpTimeBound in LALSimulation, which drops the negative terms so that it never underestimates: $\(T_{\text{chirp}} = \frac{5M}{256\,\eta\,v^8}\left[1 + \left(\frac{743}{252} + \frac{11}{3}\eta\right)v^2 + \frac{226}{15}\chi\,v^3 + \left(\frac{3058673}{508032} + \frac{5429}{504}\eta + \frac{617}{72}\eta^2\right)v^4\right], \quad v = (\pi M f_{\text{start}})^{1/3}.\)$ Here \(\chi\) is the larger of the two spin magnitudes, taken from the spin components the waveform declares (s1_x, s1_y, s1_z, s2_x, s2_y, s2_z), or 1 if it declares none. For aligned-spin waveforms this is LAL's value; for precessing ones the full spin vector is used instead of its \(z\) component, which can only make the estimate longer.
  • Starting frequency. \(f_{\text{start}} = 2 f_{\min} / m_{\max}\), with \(f_{\min}\) the lower end of the frequency range of the data and \(m_{\max}\) the highest_mode of the waveform (2 for waveforms with only the 22 mode, 4 for the higher-mode ones). A harmonic with azimuthal number \(m\) reaches \(f_{\min}\) when the orbital frequency is \(f_{\min}/m\), which is earlier for larger \(m\).
  • Merger and ringdown. \(200\,M\) before the peak and \(1000\,M\) after it. LAL's merger bound is \(54\pi M \approx 170\,M\), and its ringdown bound (11 e-folds) goes from \(127\,M\) at zero final spin to \(704\,M\) at 0.998.
  • Padding. One cycle at \(f_{\text{start}}\), and the light travel time from the geocentre to a detector, at most \(R_\oplus/c \approx 21\) ms.

For a binary with chirp mass 28 and symmetric mass ratio 0.24 observed from 20 Hz, this gives about 1.3 s before the peak for no spin and 1.5 s for maximal spin, and about 0.4 s after it.

items.title: What it does not cover
items.text:
• It estimates the physical duration of the signal, not the tails that the sharp cut at \(f_{\min}\) gives in the time domain.
  • Tides, which shorten the inspiral, and eccentricity are not modelled.
  • A waveform that does not declare M_c and eta cannot be checked: inject_signal then raises, or warns with allow_wraparound=True.

items.title: Comparison with bilby
items.text: bilby.gw.detector.get_safe_signal_duration uses the same LAL chirp-time bound, with the actual spins and a default lower frequency of 10 Hz. It returns one segment length, the chirp time rounded up to a power of two with a floor of 4 s, and adds neither the merger, the ringdown nor any padding. Its check in inject_signal_into_gwpy_timeseries constructs a ValueError but never raises it.

items.title: Getting Started
items.text: This tutorial walks through a complete Jim run on a toy problem. We inject a non-spinning BBH signal using TaylorF2, fix every parameter except chirp mass (\(\mathcal{M}_c\)) and mass ratio (\(q\)), and sample just those two to keep things fast and easy to visualise.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
import logging
import warnings
import jax

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
logging.getLogger("flowMC").setLevel(logging.WARNING)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", "Wswiglal-redir-stdio")

from jimgw.core.single_event.detector import get_H1, get_L1
from jimgw.core.single_event.waveform import RippleTaylorF2
from jimgw.core.single_event.likelihood import TransientLikelihoodFD
from jimgw.core.single_event.transforms import MassRatioToSymmetricMassRatioTransform
from jimgw.core.prior import CombinePrior, UniformPrior
from jimgw.core.jim import Jim
from jimgw.samplers.config import FlowMCConfig

items.title: 1. Define injection parameters
items.text:
We use a non-spinning BBH signal with zero tidal deformability. Only M_c and q will be sampled; every other parameter is fixed to the injection value.

gps_time = 1126259462.0

injection_parameters = {
    "M_c": 30.0,
    "eta": 0.24,
    "s1_z": 0.0,
    "s2_z": 0.0,
    "lambda_1": 0.0,
    "lambda_2": 0.0,
    "d_L": 1000.0,
    "t_c": 0.0,
    "phase_c": 0.0,
    "iota": 0.4,
    "psi": 0.3,
    "ra": 1.5,
    "dec": 0.5,
}

items.title: 2. Set up detectors and inject the signal
items.text:
waveform = RippleTaylorF2(f_ref=20.0)

f_min = 20.0
f_max = 1024.0
duration = 4.0
sampling_frequency = 2 * f_max

noise_key = jax.random.key(0)

ifos = [get_H1(), get_L1()]
for ifo in ifos:
    ifo.load_and_set_psd()
    ifo.simulate_and_set_noise(
        duration=duration,
        sampling_frequency=sampling_frequency,
        trigger_time=gps_time,
        f_min=f_min,
        f_max=f_max,
        rng_key=noise_key,
    )
    ifo.inject_signal(waveform, injection_parameters)

items.title: 3. Define the prior
items.text:
We only sample M_c and q, so we only need priors for those two. The prior is defined in the prior space — the space before any likelihood transforms are applied.

prior = CombinePrior(
    [
        UniformPrior(29.0, 31.0, ["M_c"]),
        UniformPrior(0.125, 1.0, ["q"]),
    ]
)

items.title: 4. Define transforms
items.text:
Likelihood transforms convert parameters from the prior space to the space the waveform model expects. TaylorF2 takes \(\eta\), but we placed our prior on \(q\), so we need MassRatioToSymmetricMassRatioTransform to map \(q\) to \(\eta\) before the likelihood is evaluated.

Sample transforms convert parameters from the sampling space to the prior space. Leaving this list empty means the sampler operates directly in the prior space. You can add transforms here to reparameterise into a space that is easier to sample (e.g. unbounded coordinates, decorrelated parameters), without changing the prior definition.

likelihood_transforms = [MassRatioToSymmetricMassRatioTransform]

sample_transforms = []  # sampler operates directly in prior space (M_c, q)

items.title: 5. Build the likelihood
items.text:
All parameters that are not being sampled (or transformed) must be baked into the likelihood via fixed_parameters.

fixed_parameters = {
    k: v for k, v in injection_parameters.items() if k not in ["M_c", "eta"]
}

likelihood = TransientLikelihoodFD(
    ifos,
    waveform=waveform,
    f_min=f_min,
    f_max=f_max,
    fixed_parameters=fixed_parameters,
)

items.title: 6. Sample with Jim
items.text:
With only two parameters, we scale everything down from the defaults: fewer chains, fewer loops, and a smaller normalizing flow to keep compilation and runtime short.

jim = Jim(
    likelihood,
    prior,
    sampler_config=FlowMCConfig(
        n_chains=100,
        n_local_steps=50,
        n_global_steps=100,
        n_training_loops=5,
        n_production_loops=3,
        n_epochs=5,
        rq_spline_hidden_units=[32, 32],
        rq_spline_n_layers=4,
        rq_spline_n_bins=8,
        n_max_examples=3000,
    ),
    sample_transforms=sample_transforms,
    likelihood_transforms=likelihood_transforms,
)

jim.sample()

items.title: 7. Inspect the results
items.text:
The corner plot shows the 1-D and 2-D marginal posteriors for the two sampled parameters. The dashed lines mark the injected (true) values.

from corner import corner
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

samples = jim.get_samples()

fig = corner(
    np.column_stack([samples["M_c"], samples["q"]]),
    labels=[r"$\mathcal{M}_c\ [M_\odot]$", r"$q$"],
    truths=[
        injection_parameters["M_c"],
        MassRatioToSymmetricMassRatioTransform.inverse(
            {"eta": injection_parameters["eta"]}
        )[0]["q"],
    ],
)
plt.show()

items.title: Analysing GW150914 with the CLI
items.text: This tutorial walks through a complete parameter-estimation run on GW150914 — the first gravitational-wave detection — using the jim-run command. By the end you will have a posterior sample file and know how to inspect the results.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• Jim installed: pip install jimgw (or uv sync in the repository)
  • Internet access to fetch strain and PSD data from GWOSC
  • A GPU is strongly recommended; CPU runs are possible but slow

items.title: 1. Generate a template config
items.text:
jim-run --init gw150914.toml

This writes a GW150914-style template config to gw150914.toml and exits. Open it in any text editor — the sections below explain each piece.

items.title: Seed
items.text:
seed = 0

JAX random seed. Change this to run independent realisations.

items.title: [data]
items.text:
[data]
type = "gwosc"
detectors = ["H1", "L1"]
trigger_time = 1126259462.4
duration = 4.0
post_trigger_duration = 2.0
psd_duration = 1024.0
  • type = "gwosc" — fetches strain and PSD from the public GWOSC archive automatically.
  • detectors — the detectors to include. H1 is LIGO Hanford, L1 is LIGO Livingston.
  • trigger_time — GPS time of the event (1126259462.4 s for GW150914).
  • duration — analysis segment length in seconds. The strain window runs from trigger_time - duration + post_trigger_duration to trigger_time + post_trigger_duration.
  • post_trigger_duration — seconds after the trigger kept in the analysis window (2 s is standard for stellar-mass BBH).
  • psd_duration — length of the off-source segment used to estimate the PSD (1024 s is recommended to resolve low-frequency features).

items.title: [waveform]
items.text:
[waveform]
approximant = "IMRPhenomXAS"
f_ref = 20.0
  • approximant — which ripple waveform model to use. IMRPhenomXAS is a fast, accurate aligned-spin BBH model.
  • f_ref — reference frequency in Hz at which spin magnitudes and angles are defined (20 Hz is conventional for BBH).

items.title: [prior]
items.text:
[prior]
M_c     = { type = "uniform",   min = 10.0,  max = 80.0  }
q       = { type = "uniform",   min = 0.125, max = 1.0   }
s1_z    = { type = "uniform",   min = -0.99, max = 0.99  }
s2_z    = { type = "uniform",   min = -0.99, max = 0.99  }
iota    = { type = "sine" }
d_L     = { type = "power_law", min = 1.0,   max = 2000.0, alpha = 2.0 }
t_c     = { type = "uniform",   min = -0.1,  max = 0.1   }
phase_c = { type = "uniform",   min = 0.0,   max = 6.283185307179586 }
psi     = { type = "uniform",   min = 0.0,   max = 3.141592653589793 }
ra      = { type = "uniform",   min = 0.0,   max = 6.283185307179586 }
dec     = { type = "cosine" }

Each line names a parameter and specifies its prior distribution. Key choices for GW150914:

Parameter Meaning Prior choice M_c Chirp mass (\(M_\odot\)) Uniform, broad enough to encompass GW150914 (\(\sim 28\,M_\odot\)) q Mass ratio \(m_2/m_1 \leq 1\) Uniform; 0.125 = 1:8 mass ratio s1_z, s2_z Aligned spin components Uniform on (-0.99, 0.99) — physical black holes iota Inclination angle sine prior = uniform on the sphere d_L Luminosity distance (Mpc) power_law with \(\alpha=2\) = uniform in volume t_c Coalescence time offset (s) Uniform ±0.1 s around trigger_time phase_c Coalescence phase Uniform on \([0, 2\pi)\) psi Polarisation angle Uniform on \([0, \pi)\) ra, dec Sky position Uniform in ra; cosine prior in dec = uniform on sphere

The CLI automatically infers all required transforms (mass-ratio conversion, sky-frame rotation) from the parameter names — you do not configure these yourself.

items.title: [likelihood]
items.text:
[likelihood]
f_min = 20.0
f_max = 1024.0

The frequency range of the likelihood. 20–1024 Hz is standard for stellar-mass BBH with LIGO O1 data.

items.title: [sampler]
items.text:
[sampler]
type = "flowmc"
n_chains = 1000
n_local_steps = 100
n_global_steps = 1000
n_training_loops = 50
n_production_loops = 10
n_NFproposal_batch_size = 100
global_thinning = 100

flowmc is a normalizing-flow-enhanced MCMC sampler. For a quick test (minutes instead of hours), reduce to:

n_chains = 100
n_global_steps = 100
n_production_loops = 2

items.title: [output]
items.text:
[output]
dir = "output/GW150914"
save_corner = false

Results are written to output/GW150914/. Set save_corner = true to automatically generate a corner plot (requires the corner package).

items.title: 3. Run the analysis
items.text:
jim-run gw150914.toml

Use -v for verbose (DEBUG-level) logging. On a modern GPU the production settings finish in roughly 30–60 minutes; the quick-test settings complete in a few minutes.

Expected console output:

INFO | jimgw.cli | Loaded config from gw150914.toml
INFO | jimgw.cli | seed: 0
INFO | jimgw.cli | data: type=gwosc, detectors=['H1', 'L1']
INFO | jimgw.cli | waveform: IMRPhenomXAS (f_ref=20.0 Hz)
INFO | jimgw.cli | prior: 11 parameter(s): ['M_c', 'q', 's1_z', ...]
INFO | jimgw.cli | sampler: type=flowmc
INFO | jimgw.cli | Sampling complete.

items.title: 4. Inspect the outputs
items.text:
After the run, output/GW150914/ contains:

output/GW150914/
├── samples.npz          # posterior samples
├── diagnostics.json     # scalar diagnostics (acceptance rates, …)
├── diagnostics.npz      # array diagnostics (log-prob traces, …)
└── config.final.toml    # the resolved config (useful for reproducing this run)

items.title: Load the posterior samples
items.text:
import numpy as np

data    = np.load("output/GW150914/samples.npz")
params  = list(data.keys())                          # one key per parameter
samples = np.column_stack([data[p] for p in params]) # shape: (n_samples, n_params)

print(params)
# ['M_c', 'q', 's1_z', 's2_z', 'iota', 'd_L', 't_c', 'phase_c', 'psi', 'ra', 'dec']

items.title: Make a corner plot
items.text:
import corner
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig = corner.corner(samples, labels=params)
plt.savefig("corner.png", dpi=150)

items.title: Reproduce the run
items.text:
config.final.toml records the exact resolved configuration (including any defaults that were applied). To reproduce the run, pass it directly to jim-run. Because config.final.toml retains the original output.dir, the run will abort if that directory already exists and output.overwrite is not set. Before re-running, either change output.dir to a new path or add output.overwrite = true:

# in config.final.toml — pick one:
[output]
dir = "output/GW150914_repro"   # write to a fresh directory
# or
overwrite = true                # allow overwriting output/GW150914 in-place

Then run:

jim-run output/GW150914/config.final.toml

items.title: 5. Next steps
items.text:
• Switch to a nested sampler — change [sampler] to type = "blackjax-ns-aw" or type = "blackjax-nss" to obtain a log-evidence estimate.
  • Try an injection — change [data] to type = "injection" with injection_parameters and a noise_seed to validate recovery on a known signal. See the CLI Config Reference for the full injection syntax.
  • Enable heterodyning — add a [likelihood.heterodyne] block for a 10–100× likelihood speedup. See the CLI Config Reference.
  • Full config reference — CLI Config Reference documents every available field and default.
